questions.q: A factory produces 500 items, 20 of which are defective. What is the probability that a randomly selected item is non-defective?
questions.a: n = 500, defective = 20, non-defective = 480. P(non-defective) = 480/500 = 24/25 = 0.96. A wrong answer (e.g., 20/500 = 1/25) shows the student computed P(defective) instead of P(non-defective).

questions.q: In a class of 40 students, 25 play cricket and 15 play football. If one student is selected at random, what is the probability that the student plays cricket?
questions.a: n = 40, favourable (cricket) = 25. P(cricket) = 25/40 = 5/8. A wrong answer (e.g., 25/15) shows the student used the wrong denominator or confused the favourable count with the other category.

questions.q: A weather forecast says there is a 60% chance of rain tomorrow. Interpret this in terms of probability.
questions.a: P(rain) = 0.60, meaning that in 60 out of 100 similar weather situations, it rained. It does NOT mean it will rain for 60% of the day. A wrong answer (e.g., "it will rain for 14.4 hours") shows a fundamental misunderstanding of probability interpretation.

questions.q: A lottery has 100 tickets, and you buy 5. What is the probability that you do NOT win?
questions.a: P(win) = 5/100 = 1/20. P(not win) = 1 − 1/20 = 19/20 = 0.95. A wrong answer (e.g., 95/100 = 19/20 without showing the complement step) is correct numerically but misses the reasoning.

questions.q: Why is probability useful in real-life decision-making?
questions.a: Probability quantifies uncertainty, allowing rational decisions under risk. Examples: insurance companies set premiums based on accident probabilities, doctors assess treatment success rates, quality control teams decide batch acceptance based on defect rates. Without probability, decisions would be based on intuition rather than data. A wrong answer (e.g., "it tells you what will happen") shows a misunderstanding — probability gives likelihood, not certainty.

questions.q: A survey of 200 people found 80 prefer tea, 70 prefer coffee, and 50 prefer juice. If one person is selected, what is the probability they prefer neither tea nor coffee?
questions.a: Neither tea nor coffee = juice = 50. P = 50/200 = 1/4. Alternatively: P(tea or coffee) = (80 + 70)/200 = 150/200 = 3/4. P(neither) = 1 − 3/4 = 1/4. A wrong answer (e.g., 80/200 = 2/5) shows the student computed P(tea) instead of P(neither).
